summary: Discusses directions for the possible future evolution of the Internet architecture and suggests steps toward desired goals. It is an informational discussion document rather than a protocol specification, written when concerns about growth and addressing were mounting.

plainLanguage.summary: This RFC records a 1991 discussion about how the Internet might need to change as it grows. It identifies five areas for planning, but does not define a new protocol.

subtitle: An Internet architecture discussion that identifies growth, routing, security, and application challenges for future work.

tldr.problem: Internet growth was putting pressure on the existing architecture, including addressing and routing, while new networks, security needs, and applications were emerging.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC records assumptions about the future Internet and identifies five areas for architectural evolution: routing and addressing, multiple protocol suites, security, traffic control and state, and advanced applications.
tldr.outcome: It proposes planning and research directions for discussion. It is an informational document, not a protocol specification.

today: RFC 1287 is an Informational RFC published in December 1991, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It presents discussion and proposed directions, not a specification for a protocol.

sections.title: Assumptions and Planning Priorities
sections.content:
The IAB and IESG discussed architectural issues in January and June 1991. They assumed that TCP/IP and OSI would coexist for a long time, that the Internet would continue to connect diverse networks and services, and that public and private networks would both be part of it.

The document identifies five areas for future work: routing and addressing, support for multiple protocol suites, security architecture, traffic control and state, and advanced applications. It is based on reports from groups at the Architecture Retreat and was offered for discussion and comment.
sections.plainLanguage: The authors expect different network technologies and protocol suites to coexist. They identify five areas where the Internet's architecture may need to evolve.

sections.title: Routing and Addressing
sections.content:
The RFC expects the Internet to run out of some classes of IP network addresses and eventually the available 32-bit address space, given the way it is then subdivided and managed. It also warns that the number of network numbers could exceed what routing algorithms can handle.

The proposed direction is to aggregate network numbers into larger routing units such as Autonomous Systems or Administrative Domains. The RFC also discusses three address-format choices: reuse the 32-bit field with local meaning, expand the field to 64 bits and include a domain, or use a larger flat host identifier with connection setup mapping it to a domain. It says migration must be planned alongside scalable routing and network management.
sections.plainLanguage: The authors expect the address space and routing tables to become difficult to manage. They propose grouping networks into larger routing units and planning a broad migration rather than relying only on small changes.

sections.title: A Multi-Protocol Internet
sections.content:
The document asks how the Internet should support more than one protocol suite and whether partial or filtered connectivity should be part of the architecture. It distinguishes physical link sharing between suites that do not interoperate from application interoperability through relays or user agents.

It proposes a process-based view with four parts: a TCP/IP core, link sharing, application interoperability, and hybridization or integration. The authors describe the latter parts as ways to expand the Internet while noting that they add complexity, cost, management work, and sometimes lost functionality.
sections.plainLanguage: Different protocol suites may share physical links without communicating directly, or applications may relay information between them. The RFC also considers combining compatible parts of different architectures.

sections.title: Security Architecture
sections.content:
The RFC says Internet security architecture should favor simplicity, testability, clear trust assumptions, appropriate technology, and defined security perimeters. It considers protection at link, network or subnet, host, and process or application levels, each with different assumptions about which components are trusted.

Desired services include authenticatable names, access control, integrity, confidentiality, and denial-of-service prevention. The document calls for a security reference model and further work on directory services, certificates, distributed-system security, and application-level security.
sections.plainLanguage: Security needs to be designed for a clear boundary, such as a link, host, or application. The RFC calls for simple, testable protections and a way to connect names with public keys and permissions.

sections.title: Traffic Control and Advanced Applications
sections.content:
The then-current Internet treats IP datagrams as best effort, while the RFC expects future voice and video applications to need performance guarantees. It calls for research into router traffic control, resource setup and state, how resource reservations relate to routing, multicast models, and accounting.

Advanced applications also need common formats for exchanging text, images, graphics, video, audio, display information, and data objects. The document lists needs such as store-and-forward, global file systems, inter-process communication, data broadcast, and database access. It notes that these applications also depend on real-time delivery, authentication, and access control.
sections.plainLanguage: Voice and video may need more than best-effort delivery, so routers may need traffic controls and resource state. Applications also need shared ways to represent and exchange different kinds of information.
